hero.description: This is not one attraction but a day through the landscape that grows most of Laos' coffee: Paksong, plantations, processing stops and waterfalls all belong to the same plateau.
steps: Leave Pakse with a simple route
Keep enough time for the road back
hero.rhythmNote: Build the day around understanding the plateau, not collecting pins. One good coffee visit and one contrasting waterfall can tell you more than six rushed stops.

time.secondary: a useful day route from Pakse; longer loops go beyond this card

budget.secondary: cost depends on vehicle, tastings and chosen attractions

chapters.label: THE COFFEE
chapters.title: Coffee is the landscape, not a souvenir at the end
chapters.body: The Lao Coffee Association places about 95 percent of national coffee production in three districts on the Bolaven Plateau, with Paksong at the centre of the visitor route. That matters because a good stop should connect the cup to the place: altitude, farms, harvest, processing and the people working between them.

chapters.label: THE ROUTE
chapters.title: Fewer stops make a better plateau day
chapters.body: From Pakse, the useful version is a full day rather than a race around every named waterfall. Pick one coffee stop where you can actually learn something, then add one or two landscapes that feel different. Tad Fane is the big gorge view; Tad Yuang is the closer walk. The road between them is part of the experience.

note.label: ATLAS NOTE
note.text: A coffee route should answer one question by the end of the day: why does so much Lao coffee come from this plateau?

chapters.label: HARVEST
chapters.title: November to March changes what you can see
chapters.body: The Lao Coffee Association gives November to March as the broad harvest season. That is when farms and processing activity are easiest to connect to the final cup. Outside harvest, the route still works, but choose a producer that can explain cultivation and processing rather than expecting field activity everywhere.

chapters.label: CHOICE
chapters.title: Do not confuse the day route with the full Bolaven Loop
chapters.body: This card is the Pakse-based version: out toward Paksong, coffee country and selected waterfalls, then back. The longer motorbike loop reaches farther into the plateau and deserves its own time. Trying to compress that larger journey into one day usually turns the coffee stops into scenery.

beforeYouLeave.title: Decide what the day is about before you leave Pakse
beforeYouLeave.body: If coffee is the priority, protect time for a farm, cooperative or producer visit and let waterfalls support the route. If scenery is the priority, reverse the balance. The plateau is broad enough that an unedited list quickly becomes a driving day.

note.label: GOOD RULE
note.text: One meaningful coffee stop + one or two contrasting landscapes is already a full day.

items.label: Format
items.detail: Paksong is the useful centre of gravity for a coffee-focused day on the plateau.

items.label: Coffee season
items.detail: This is the strongest period for seeing harvest and processing activity, though farms and tastings can operate outside it.

items.label: Stop selection
items.detail: A producer or cooperative visit plus one or two waterfalls is enough to give the day a clear shape.

items.label: Budget
items.detail: The road itself is not a single ticketed attraction. Budget for transport, any farm or tasting fees and the entrance fees of waterfall sites you choose.

faq.question: Is the Bolaven Plateau Coffee Route one official attraction?
faq.answer: No. Think of it as a Pakse-based day route through coffee country, with Paksong as the main centre and individual farms, producers and waterfalls chosen along the way.

faq.question: When is the coffee harvest on the Bolaven Plateau?
faq.answer: The Lao Coffee Association gives November to March as the broad harvest season. That is the most useful window if you want to connect the farms with active processing.

faq.question: How many coffee and waterfall stops should I plan in one day?
faq.answer: Fewer than the map suggests. One substantial coffee stop and one or two contrasting waterfalls usually produces a better day than rushing through every name on the plateau.

faq.question: Can I include Tad Fane and Tad Yuang on a coffee day?
faq.answer: Yes. They are a useful pair because Tad Fane is mainly a gorge panorama while Tad Yuang gives you a closer walking experience around the falls.

faq.question: Is this the same as doing the full Bolaven Loop?
faq.answer: No. This card describes a full-day route from Pakse into the Paksong coffee area. The wider Bolaven Loop reaches farther and is better treated as a separate multi-day journey.
